opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I'd frame it is that most people who come to fine-tuning don't actually have a data problem they can articulate yet. They have a task. They know they want the model to, say, extract fields from insurance documents or answer questions in their company's tone, and the data is kind of the missing middle. So a good curation tool should meet them there.

Concretely, I'd say a few things. First, generation. A lot of the time you don't have enough labeled examples, so you want to be able to synthesize data, using a strong model to produce examples, maybe seeded from a handful of real ones or from your documents. But generation alone is the easy part. The harder part is the second thing, which is diversity. If you just prompt a model a thousand times, you get a thousand slightly different versions of the same example. So the tool should help you structure the space, break the task into subtopics, vary difficulty, vary formats, so you actually cover the distribution you care about.

Third is quality filtering. You need ways to score and filter, whether that's LLM-as-a-judge, heuristics, deduplication, checking for correctness when you can verify it, like running code or checking math. Throwing away bad data often matters more than adding more data.

And then fourth, I think people underrate the engineering side. When you're making hundreds of thousands of model calls, you need batching, caching, retries, cost tracking, being able to resume a pipeline if it fails halfway. That's honestly where a lot of the pain is in practice.

And finally, it should close the loop with evaluation. You curate data, you fine-tune, you evaluate, you look at where the model fails, and then you go back and generate or curate more data for those failure modes. Data curation isn't a one-shot step; it's iterative, and the tool should make that loop fast.

r001.rationale: The response discusses structuring task coverage through subtopics, difficulty, and formats, but does not propose structured model outputs guiding curation stages.

r002.rationale: It says the tool needs retries for pipelines making hundreds of thousands of model calls, indicating retries should be handled by the tool.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that when people fine-tune a model, they tend to spend maybe ten percent of their time on the actual training and ninety percent on the data. And most of that ninety percent is this very manual, ad hoc loop: write a bunch of prompts, generate some responses, eyeball them, notice a problem, filter, regenerate, repeat. So a data curation tool should really be taking that whole loop and making it systematic.

Concretely, I think there are a few pieces. The first is just getting data in and looking at it. That sounds trivial, but a lot of people never actually look at their data at the example level, and when they do, they find duplicates, formatting issues, label noise, things that are just wrong. So the tool should make inspection easy, with some help from a model to surface the weird stuff, cluster it, flag outliers.

The second is generation. For most fine-tuning use cases today you're not going to have enough human-written examples, so you're going to be doing synthetic data. And the hard part there isn't calling an LLM, it's getting diversity and coverage. If you just ask a model for a thousand examples, you get a thousand slight variations of the same three things. So the tool needs to help you structure that: seed from real data, vary along explicit axes, cover the long tail of your task distribution, and not collapse into mode.

Third is quality and filtering. Not every generated example should make it into the training set. You want scoring, whether that's a judge model, rules, or human review, and you want to be able to express what good looks like for your task, because it's different for a coding assistant versus a customer support bot.

And then the last piece, which I think gets overlooked, is closing the loop with evaluation. You should be able to train, see where the model fails, and have those failures feed back into what data you generate next. Data curation isn't a one-shot preprocessing step, it's iterative, and the tool should treat it that way. If it just gives you a cleaned CSV and walks away, it's missed the point.

r001.rationale: The response recommends structuring generation around explicit axes and using models to inspect data, but it does not propose structured model outputs to guide curation stages.

r002.rationale: It describes repeated generation and regeneration, but does not say the tool should manage retries for users generating examples at large scale.

astra-6.text:
I think a data curation tool should help you figure out what data your model actually needs. If you’re fine-tuning for a particular use case, you want to understand what’s in your dataset, whether it represents that use case, and where the gaps are. Are there duplicates? Are there incorrect labels? Are there important examples that you’re missing?

And ideally, it should connect that back to model performance. You evaluate the model, find the kinds of examples it struggles with, and then use that information to decide what to collect or label next. So it’s not just about cleaning up a dataset once. It’s about making that iteration—between your data and your model—much easier.

r001.rationale: The response uses model performance and failure examples to guide what data to collect or label next, but it does not mention structured model outputs guiding curation stages.

r002.rationale: The response does not address generating fine-tuning examples at scale or managing retries.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it should help you answer a few basic questions: What data do I have, what’s actually useful for the task, and what am I missing? If you’re fine-tuning a model, you don’t necessarily want to throw all your data at it. You want relevant examples, good coverage of the cases you care about, and labels you can trust.

So the tool should help you find duplicates, identify mislabeled or ambiguous examples, and understand where your dataset is overrepresented or underrepresented. And then it should connect that back to model performance. If the model is failing on a particular slice, can you find the examples that would help address that failure? To me, that feedback loop—from data to model behavior and back to data—is a really important part of curation.

r001.rationale: The response discusses selecting, checking, and balancing examples, but does not propose using structured model outputs to guide curation stages.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention generating examples at scale or handling retries for users.
